newsitem.title: FRANCE: ATHLETICS-OTTEY PULLS OUT OF WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-OTTEY PULLS OUT OF WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS.

text.p: Merlene Ottey has pulled out of the world indoor championships because of a back injury and will not defend her 60 metres title in the three-day competition starting on Friday.
Ottey sustained the injury while training in Rome, leaving American Gail Devers, who beat the Jamaican on a photo-finish in last year's Olympic 100 metres final, as the race favourite.
Devers clocked the year's fastest time, an even seven seconds, at the U.S. trials in Atlanta last Saturday.
Her closest rivals in a race in which one minor mistake can mean the difference between finishing first or last are likely to be Russian Irinva Privalova and Nigeria's Christy Opara.
Privalova has a splendid record at the world indoor championships, winning the 60 metres title in 1991, the 200 in 1993 and the 400 two years ago.
Trinidad's Ato Boldon, equal fastest in the world this year over 60 metres, has opted to run the 200 only because of a schedule which makes a 60-200 metres double virtually impossible.
Boldon is the world leader over 200 with a time of 20.35 at the Birmingham grand prix last month.
The introduction of prize money and world record bonuses for the first time at a world championships has clearly attracted several athletes who might not otherwise have competed here.
One of these is Denmark's Kenyan-born 800 metres outdoor champion Wilson Kipketer, who has not even run indoors this northern winter.
Kipketer, who has lived in Denmark since 1990, was not allowed to compete for his adopted country at last year's Atlanta Olympics.
Another is Ireland's world 5,000 metres champion Sonia O'Sullivan, who has not raced indoors for five years and who has been racing outdoors in Australia this year.
The race of the championships could come in the men's 3,000 metres between Ethiopia's world record holder Haile Gebrselassie and Kenya's world steeplechase champion Moses Kiptanui.

Gebrselassie refused to comment on the possibility of a world record at a news conference on Thursday but Kiptanui has already indicated the pace could be fast to burn off such fine runners as Germany's 1992 Olympic 5,000 metres champion Dieter Baumann.
The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) will pay $50,000 to race winners plus bonuses also of $50,000 for any athlete breaking a world record.
One man who could earn himself $100,000 is Cuban triple jumper Eliecer Urrutia, who improved the world mark to 17.83 metres in Sindelfingen, Germany, last Saturday.
Little is known about Urrutia outside Cuba and the man himself did not greatly add to the sum of human knowledge on Thursday.
"I come from a province in Cuba," he said. "I have been training with the national team for four years. My ambition is to be on the podium at these championships."

IAAF president Primo Nebiolo, talking at a televised news conference in Lausanne where he is attending a meeting of the International Olympic Committee, said prize money was now essential to reward athletes for the sacrifices they made for their sport.
"We are starting a new era in athletics," he said.
His words were echoed by Devers.
"Maybe it will keep our sport from dying," she said.
